Solar Power Helps Farmers in Kenya

Farmers in western Kenya are using small solar-powered pumps to water their crops. The pumps take the place of costly diesel engines. Many farmers say the change has increased their harvests and reduced their costs.

James Otieno grows vegetables near Lake Victoria. He said diesel fuel used to take almost half of his profits. Now, he uses a solar pump that a local company installed last year. The device pulls water from a nearby stream and moves it through pipes to his fields.

Aid groups have helped bring solar technology to rural areas across East Africa. They say solar pumps are cheaper to run and better for the environment than fuel-powered machines. The pumps also do not produce the noise or smoke that diesel engines create.

Some farmers worried that the new equipment would be too expensive to buy. But local banks have started offering small loans so farmers can pay for the pumps over time. Otieno said he expects to finish paying off his pump within two years.

Experts say the project could serve as a model for other developing regions that face similar water and energy problems.

Community Garden Opens in London Park

A new community garden has opened in a park in east London. Local families and school children helped to plant vegetables and flowers over the past month.

The garden was started by a small charity called Green Steps. The group wanted to give people without gardens a place to grow their own food. Anyone who lives nearby can ask for a small plot of land to use.

Sarah Lin, a teacher at a local primary school, brought her students to help dig the soil and plant seeds. She said the children learned about where food comes from and how plants grow.

The charity plans to hold a harvest festival in the autumn. Visitors will be able to taste vegetables grown in the garden and learn simple cooking tips.

Organizers hope the project will encourage more people across the city to start similar gardens in their own neighborhoods.

Welcome to this week's Learning English report. Today we're visiting a new community garden in east London.

The garden opened last month in a small park that used to be an empty field. It was created by a charity called Green Steps, which wanted to give local families a place to grow their own vegetables and flowers.

Anyone who lives in the neighborhood can apply for a small plot of land. Since the garden opened, more than thirty families have signed up to start growing plants there.

Sarah Lin teaches at a primary school nearby. She brought a group of her students to help prepare the soil and plant seeds earlier this month. She told us the children were excited to get their hands dirty and learn where their food actually comes from.

Lin said many children today have never seen vegetables growing before they end up on a plate. Working in the garden, she said, helps them understand the connection between farming and the food they eat every day.

The charity is now planning a harvest festival for the autumn. Visitors will be able to walk through the garden, taste fresh vegetables, and pick up simple tips for cooking with what they grow.

Organizers say they hope this small garden will inspire people in other parts of the city to start similar projects in their own neighborhoods.

That's our report for this week. Thanks for listening.

New Study Looks at Sleep Habits of Teenagers

A new study from researchers in Australia looks at how much sleep teenagers actually get compared to how much they need. The study followed more than one thousand students between the ages of thirteen and eighteen for six months.

Researchers found that most teenagers slept far less than the eight to ten hours recommended by sleep experts. Many students reported staying awake late at night using phones or computers, even on school nights.

Doctor Amara Osei, who led the study, said poor sleep can affect a teenager's mood, memory, and ability to concentrate in class. She said schools and parents often underestimate how serious the problem has become.

The research team suggested several changes that might help, including starting school later in the morning and limiting screen use before bedtime. Some schools in the study area have already begun testing later start times.

Osei said early results from those schools appear promising, with students reporting better focus and fewer complaints of tiredness during the day. The full findings will be published later this year in a medical journal.

This is a VOA Learning English health report. A new study from researchers in Australia has looked closely at teenage sleep habits.

The study followed more than one thousand students between the ages of thirteen and eighteen over a period of six months. Researchers asked the students to record when they went to bed, when they woke up, and how they felt during the school day.

The results showed that most teenagers in the study slept far less than the eight to ten hours that sleep experts recommend for their age group. Many students said they stayed awake late at night using their phones or computers, even when they had school the next morning.

Doctor Amara Osei led the research team. She said that poor sleep can affect a teenager's mood, memory, and ability to concentrate during class. She added that schools and parents often underestimate just how serious the problem has become for young people today.

Based on the findings, the research team suggested a few changes that might help. These include starting the school day later in the morning and limiting screen use before bedtime. A small number of schools in the study area have already begun testing later start times as an experiment.

Osei said the early results from those schools look promising. Students at those schools have reported better focus during lessons and fewer complaints of tiredness throughout the day.

The complete findings from the study will be published later this year in a medical journal. Researchers hope the results will encourage more schools to consider changing their schedules.

row_too_short: Solar Power Helps Farmers in Kenya

Farmers in western Kenya are using small solar-powered pumps to water their crops. The pumps take the place of costly diesel engines. Many farmers say the change has increased their harvests and reduced their costs.

James Otieno grows vegetables near Lake Victoria. He said diesel fuel used to take almost half of his profits. Now, he uses a solar pump that a local company installed last year. The device pulls water from a nearby stream and moves it through pipes to his fields.

Aid groups have helped bring solar technology to rural areas across East Africa. They say solar pumps are cheaper to run and better for the environment than fuel-powered machines. The pumps also do not produce the noise or smoke that diesel engines create.

Some farmers worried that the new equipment would be too expensive to buy. But local banks have started offering small loans so farmers can pay for the pumps over time. Otieno said he expects to finish paying off his pump within two years.

Experts say the project could serve as a model for other developing regions that face similar water and energy problems.

material: AI Tutors Help Students Focus, Researchers Say

A new generation of AI-powered tutoring tools is helping some students stay focused during online lessons, according to researchers at a university in Canada. The tools track how long a student looks at the screen and gently prompt them when their attention drifts.

The research team studied more than two hundred high school students over one semester. Students who used the AI tutor reported fewer distractions and said they finished homework assignments more quickly than before.

Not every teacher is convinced the tools are worth the cost. Some worry that constant prompts could make students anxious rather than focused. The research team says more studies are needed before schools adopt the technology widely.
